storm.summary_layperson: Thunderstorms roughly 35 miles northwest are drifting toward the region and should reach the cove around 9:30 PM, by which time the Sound's cooling effect will have faded for the evening, so this one likely won't get the usual break that afternoon storms get from the water.
storm.local_effect_blurb: Marine layer holds a strong 12°F air-water gap at 5 PM, but it fades below the 5°F protective threshold by about 9:16 PM — the tracked cell isn't due until 9:30 PM, after that buffer is gone.
storm.detail_html:
KOKX radar shows a cluster of cells (up to 60 dBZ) 36–49 miles NNW/NW of the cove, drifting ESE at roughly 10 kt. The atmosphere is primed for strong convection: CAPE of 2,700 J/kg with 24 kt of bulk shear, an environment the NWS Area Forecast Discussion specifically flags for an "iso-sct pulse strong to severe threat in the high CAPE weak shear environment" this evening.

The cove's usual defense is the Long Island Sound marine layer — right now the water sits at 72.7°F against 84.2°F air, an 11.5°F gap that would normally slow or weaken an incoming cell. But that gap is a trend, not a fixed condition: as the air cools after sunset (8:04 PM) while the Sound holds steady, the gap narrows below the ~5°F protective threshold around 9:16 PM.

The nearest tracked cell is 38.5 miles NNW, closing at 8.4 kt, with an ETA of about 9:30 PM (window 8:30–10:30 PM). That's after the marine-layer buffer collapses (projected gap 4.7°F at arrival) and after the sea breeze has also died for the evening, so no local mechanism is discounting this storm. Expect it to hit the cove at close to full strength — similar to what inland towns will see — rather than the softened version the Sound often delivers on hotter mid-afternoon days.

What would change the call: a cell that arrived before roughly 9:16 PM would still get the marine-layer discount and likely weaken crossing the Sound. The AFD also flags potential for a "more organized line" developing into the region later in the evening — if a stronger cell organizes and closes inside 25 miles at ≥45 dBZ, or a severe thunderstorm warning is issued, risk would escalate to high.

arrival.blurb: Radar-tracked cell 39 mi NNW closing at 8 kt, arriving after the marine layer fades — expect it at full strength.

wind.tactics_blurb: SSW sea breeze reinforced by a region-wide southerly gradient — steady through the middle of the window before easing after the 8:04 PM sunset. Pressure is fairly even across the cove with a slight edge to the east side; start mid-line and play the oscillations while the sea breeze is mature.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
Both ingredients for a sea breeze are in place: an 11.5°F air-water temperature gap (well above the 5°F gate) and a synoptic gradient that's onshore (southerly, ensemble median SSW) at 9.1 kt — under the 15 kt ceiling for reinforcement rather than opposition. That combination makes this a sea-breeze-reinforced-by-gradient day, not a pure thermal day: expect it stronger and steadier through the window than a thermal alone would produce, and holding roughly 30–60 minutes past the normal sunset collapse because the gradient flow persists after the thermal itself dies.

HRRR's raw surface direction (S, 177°) is running well behind the real sea breeze — western-LIS stations are already reading SW (222°), a 45° divergence. The fetcher's maturation correction adds 15° of veer for the next few hours, putting the corrected forecast at SSW (192°); that's the direction used for the 17:00–19:00 rows above. After the thermal fades near sunset, the remaining flow is gradient-driven and the raw HRRR direction (S–SSW, 187–210°) is used directly.

Cove geography: SSW flow runs cleanly up the cove's N–S axis with only slight channeling along the west shore. Pressure should stay fairly uniform, with a small edge to the east side (off Tod's Point) where there's less shelter — favor the right side of the beat on average, but this is not a sharply lopsided day.

Shift character: expect persistent right-veering shifts in the first hour or two as the sea breeze is still maturing, transitioning to normal 10–20° oscillations by 18:00–19:00 once it's fully established. After sunset the wind eases and direction may wander more as the gradient alone takes over and the boundary layer stabilizes.

On the water: 6–8 kt through the first half of the window sits in the sweet spot for one-design dinghies — good, raceable pressure. By 21:00–22:00, speeds drop toward the 3–5 kt drifter range as the thermal component is gone and only a light gradient remains; the last race of a series could turn finicky. No postponement risk expected, but don't count on big breeze late.
